latin.2415: XXVI. Praeterea multi Scholae Reformatae Theologi gratiam distinguere solent in gratiam Universalem, & gratiam particularem: sed non omnes eodem sensu. Polanus syntagmatis sui libro 2. capite 21. postquam initio capitis distinxit gratiam in eam quae in Deo residet, & eam quae a Deo data est, sub finem ait, Gratia hominibus a Deo data vel universalis est, ut tum gratia naturalis quae omnibus & singulis hominibus datur, tum gratia supernaturalis ante lapsum: vel particularis, ut gratia supernaturalis post lapsum, quae parti duntaxat humani generis confertur.
latin.2416: XXVII. Nam antea distinxit gratiam in naturalem, & supernaturalem. Et per gratiam naturalem intelligit ipsam naturam, & dona omnia tum naturae integrae, tum quae in natura corrupta remanserunt. Per gratiam vero supernaturalem dona quaecunque supra naturam hominibus a Deo collata. Ideoque rursus gratiam supernaturalem distinguit in gratiam supernaturalem ante lapsum hominis, per quam designat dona supra naturam homini integro collata: & in gratiam supernaturalem post lapsum hominis, quo nomine complectitur omnia dona supra naturam homini peccatori collata.
latin.2417: XXVIII. Itaque per gratiam universalem significat dona tam naturalia, quam supernaturalia ante peccatum primis parentibus collata, quia scilicet pertinebant ad totum genus humanum, quod illis solis constabat, & in omnes eorum posteros propaganda erant, si perstitissent in Dei obsequio. Et praeterea post humani generis corruptionem, beneficia & dona naturae quae post peccatum remanserunt, & sunt omnibus hominibus communia, vult quoque posse nomine universalis gratiae designari. Sed post peccatum nullum donum sive beneficium supernaturale vult esse universale. Et idcirco post lapsum omnem gratiam supernaturalem dicit esse particularem. Ac propterea gratiam quam particularem vocat, distinguit in eam quae communis est electis & reprobis, & quae a Deo datur ad aliorum salutem, qualia sunt charismata quae dicuntur a Scholasticis gratiae gratis datae: & in eam quae est electorum propria, & destinata est ad salutem eorum quibus datur, ut sunt fides, regeneratio, resipiscentia, charitas, spes vitae aeternae, donum perseverantiae, quae Scholastici revocant ad gratiam gratum facientem.
latin.2418: XXIX. Paulus vero Testardus ante aliquot annos Blaesensis Ecclesiae Pastor in synopsi doctrinae de natura & gratia, thesi 300. distinctionem gratiae in Particularem & Universalem sensu longe diverso usurpat. Nam, inquit, gratia erga peccatores duplex est, Generalis, & Particularis. Generalis quae toti mundo datur, Oblatio & facultas salutis. Particularis quae est Electorum tantum, salutis applicatio. Cujus fundamentum proximum est electio libera: medium vocatio efficax: corona justificatio, custodia, glorificatio. Et statim gratiam illam particularem dicit esse vel praevenientem, qualis est Electio & Vocatio: Vel misericorditer remunerantem, qualis est justificatio, custodia, glorificatio.
latin.2419: XXX. Itaque ex ejus mente, gratia universalis sive generalis est illud Dei beneficium quo salus omnibus hominibus offertur, & ita illis omnibus & singulis possibilis redditur, ut salvari possint, si velint, & per ipsos tantum stet quominus salutem adipiscantur. Censet enim Deum omnibus Christum Redemptorem parasse, & morte ejus sic expiata fuisse omnium hominum peccata, ut ex parte Dei nihil amplius obstet quominus quicunque a peccato recedit, & ad Deum convertitur, salutis fiat compos, & liberetur a perditione: cum justitiae ejus vindicatrici pro peccatis omnium hominum abunde Christi morte satisfactum fuerit. Neque id tantum, sed Deum omnes homines vocare ad salutis in Christo participationem; alios quidem expresso Evangelii verbo, alios vero voce creaturarum, & variis benignitatis & patientiae divinae testimoniis, quae in operibus naturae & providentiae relucent, hominesque ad resipiscentiam, ac consequenter ad salutem invitant.
latin.2420: XXXI. Per gratiam vero particularem intelligit illam qua Deus certos ex hominibus revera salutis participes efficit, Christi beneficium illis non simpliciter offerendo, sed efficaciter & reapse applicando. Vocat autem gratiam illam particularem, quoniam non ut prior ad omnes extenditur, sed est paucorum propria, electorum, scilicet, ut quae consistat in ipsa electione, & beneficiis inde promanantibus: qualia sunt vocatio interna & efficax, justificatio, perseverantiae donum & glorificatio.
latin.2421: XXXII. Eodem modo istam gratiae divisionem in particularem & universalem usurpat & explicat Clarissimus vir Moses Amyraldus in duobus illis tractatibus quos inscripsit, De gratia universali & particulari. Ei vero consentiunt atque astipulantur omnes ii in Gallia qui Cameronis Methodum & doctrinam sequuntur, & in Germania atque Polonia plurimi, qui pacem & concordiam cum Lutheranis quaerunt & sectantur. Verum in Belgio Reformati plerique, & in Gallia & Anglia non pauci distinctionem istam improbant & oppugnant, nec ullam admittunt Christi gratiam universalem.
latin.2422: XXXIII. Ex dictis vero satis patet, Theologos istos nomine gratiae universalis non intelligere gratiam aliquam in hominibus inhaerentem, sed tantum externum quoddam Dei beneficium, quo filium morti tradidit, ut divinae justitiae pro peccatis omnium hominum satisfieret, & quo justitia ejus ita pacata, homines extrinsecus vocat ad communionem salutis, quam Christus illis morte sua peperit. Et contra per gratiam particularem illos praecipue designare dona & auxilia Dei, quibus intus in hominibus agens in illis conversionem & fidem operatur, illosque tandem reipsa salutis aeternae participes efficit.
latin.2423: XXXIV. Unde nata est alia gratiae distinctio, in gratiam, scilicet, Objectivam atque subjectivam, quam Clarissimus ille Moses Amyraldus tradit, initio suae dissertationis de gratia Particulari. Docet enim ibi duplicem gratiam necessariam esse ad fidem in hominum animis ingenerandam. Unam quae ad modum objecti se habet, misericordiam Dei in Christi satisfactione extrinsecus offerentis: alteram quae mentem intrinsecus afficit atque illuminat, ut objectum admittatur. Priorem illam objectivam vocat, quoniam externa est, & per se nihil in homine ponit; sed solum tanquam quoddam objectum ipsi proponitur, quod fide amplecti debeat. Posteriorem vero subjectivam appellat, quoniam hominem intrinsecus immutat, & in eo tanquam in subjecto recipitur. Et Objectivam quidem istam gratiam contendit esse universalem, & ad omnes omnino homines pertinere: gratiam autem subjectivam docet esse particularem, & peculiariter electis destinatam.
latin.2424: XXXV. Porro qui in Belgio Remonstrantes dicuntur sive Arminiani, de gratia eodem fere modo Philosophantur, atque illi ex Scholae Romanae Doctoribus qui Molinistae hodie appellantur. Utuntur enim distinctionibus gratiae in excitantem atque adjuvantem, praevenientem atque subsequentem, operantem & cooperantem eodem quo illi sensu, ut videre licet in declaratione sententiae Remonstrantium circa articulum tertium & quartum, quae habetur in eorum Synodo.
latin.2425: XXXVI. Nam ibi per gratiam excitantem intelligere se dicunt gratiosam & impromeritam Dei ac Spiritus Sancti operationem, quae primum intellectum rerum salutarium cognitione imbuit, & illustrat, adeoque veritati divinae assentiri facit, & secundo in ipsam voluntatem agit per eandem illuminationem & sensus verbo comprehensos.
latin.2426: XXXVII. Addunt tamen se minime diffiteri quin Spiritus Sanctus immediate agat in voluntatem, infundendo in illam vires ac potentiam supernaturalem ad credendum, per quam tamen potentiam voluntas non necessitetur, & irresistibiliter determinetur. Hanc autem gratiam notant excitantem vocari, quia voluntatem ad assensum liberum trahit, allicit, invitat, & incitat, & homine obicem non ponente, eam actu velle facit. Et eandem quoque gratiam dici praevenientem, quia voluntatem nostram praevenit: ac denique Operantem, quia volitionis quoque causa est.
latin.2427: XXXVIII. Hujus autem gratiae necessitatem monent ex eo oriri, quod actus supernaturales, quales sunt illi in quibus consistit hominis conversio, congenitam & ingenitam voluntatis potentiam longe excedunt, ideoque viribus supernaturalibus, & speciali gratia, antecedente ipsum voluntatis actum, ad hunc eliciendum opus est; quod ad alios actus naturales voluntatis ejus potentiae proportionatos opus non est.
latin.2428: XXXIX. Adjuvans vero gratia ipsis est quae voluntatem juvat, & effective cum ea concurrit ad producendum actum; idque non moraliter tantum, sed & Physice, sive potius plusquam moraliter: quia nimirum vox Physice in hoc negotio ipsis valde incommoda videtur, propter actuum de quibus quaestio est supernaturalitatem: nec tamen occurrit alia propria vox per quam positive hoc enuncient. Atque hanc gratiam observant dici quoque cooperantem, quia cum voluntate operatur; & subsequentem respectu praevenientis & excitantis gratiae.
latin.2429: XL. Quod attinet ad distinctionem gratiae in actualem & habitualem, ea ab illis rejicitur, tanquam Scholasticorum figmentum, quod in scriptura fundamentum non habet. Modo tamen intelligatur per gratiam habitualem talis fidei, spei & charitatis in voluntatem infusio, ut citra ullam intervenientem voluntatis operationem eos habitus adipisci dicatur homo. Quippe censent per crebros fidei, spei & charitatis actus a speciali Dei gratia provenientes, tandem in nobis produci fidem, charitatem & spem habitualem: quemadmodum per iteratos actus justitiae & liberalitatis in nobis producuntur liberalitatis & justitiae habitus. Existimare vero habitus virtutum Theologicarum immediate a Deo sine propria hominis operatione produci, eorum esse qui simul & semel infundi optant omnes illos habitus, quos actibus crebris comparare nimis laboriosum esse arbitrantur.
latin.2430: XLI. Si vero per gratiam habitualem intelligere libeat potentiam quandam supernaturalem concessam voluntati ad hoc ut credere & bene agere possit, profitentur eam se lubentes admittere. Unde patet eos, licet gratiam habitualem negent, agnoscere tamen quandam qualitatem permanentem, & potentiam supernaturalem quae per gratiam infusa sit. Quod eodem fere recidit, & a sententia eorum qui aliter loquuntur, parum aut nihil differt.
latin.2431: XLII. Caeterum ex iis quae a nobis fuerunt hactenus exposita circa varias gratiae divisiones & acceptiones, tam in Schola Romana, quam in Schola Reformata, manifestum est Theologos Ecclesiae Rom. ultro docere atque concedere gratiam in scriptura sacra non semper sumi pro quibusdam Dei donis & auxiliis nobis inhaerentibus, sed per gratiam quandoque intelligi ipsum Dei favorem, unde procedunt dona & auxilia illa. Et vicissim Doctores Reformatos non negare in scriptura gratiae nomen saepe tribui divini favoris donis atque effectis. Ideoque frustra Reformati nonnulli Scholae Romanae Doctores arguunt, quasi per gratiam nunquam aliud intelligi vellent quam donum aliquod supernaturale nobis infusum. Et contra absque ratione Scholae Romanae Doctores Reformatos exagitant, & de iis queruntur, quasi nullam agnoscerent gratiam nobis inhaerentem.
latin.2432: XLIII. Praeterea patet ex dictis circa distinctionem gratiae in gratis datam & gratum facientem, non esse nisi certamen de vocibus. Nam quod Reformati contendunt nullam esse gratiam quae non gratis data sit, & omnem gratiam ideo gratiam appellari quod gratuito sit donata, admittitur a Scholae Romanae Doctoribus, qui monent quandam gratiae speciem singulariter a se dici gratiam gratis datam: non quod altera gratiae species etiam non sit gratis data; sed quia visum est Scholae conveniens speciem istam nomine generis appellare, quod proprio nomine careat.
latin.2433: XLIV. Alteram vero gratiae speciem Doctores iidem non ideo nominant gratiam gratum facientem, quod praecedat omnem actum dilectionis divinae erga nos, & sit causa qua Deus primum movetur ut nobis bene velit; id quod Reformati merito falsum & absurdum judicant: cum Deus prius diligat nos, quam illum diligamus.
latin.2434: XLV. Nec propterea tamen Schola Reformata negat id quod Romana gratiae gratum facientis nomine intelligit, fidem, scilicet, spem & charitatem esse aliquid cujus ratione homo Deo gratus & placens est singulari quodam modo, ad quem respiciens Paulus ad Hebraeos dicit, Impossibile esse sine fide placere Deo. Quo spectant Theologi Ecclesiae Romanae, dum gratiam istam gratum facientem appellant.
latin.2435: XLVI. Et sic utrique facile concedent esse aliquem divinae dilectionis actum qui praecedit illa dona & virtutes, quae Scholastici designant nomine gratiae gratum facientis: quia scilicet, Deus nobis bene vult priusquam illa habeamus: & simul esse quendam actum ejusdem dilectionis quem praecedunt ejusmodi dona, nempe quia Deo sine illis non possumus placere atque ipsi probari. Talia vero dona atque virtutes hominem qui illis ornatus est formaliter Deo gratum & placentem constituunt. Juxta illud Petri Actorum decimo, In veritate comperi quod non est personarum acceptor Deus: sed in omni gente qui timet eum, & operatur justitiam, acceptus est illi.
latin.2436: XLVII. Deinde planum est ex iis quae fuerunt ante exposita, Scholae Reformatae Doctores admittere virtutes quasdam divinitus infusas, & dona quaedam gratiae salvificae, quae sint in anima per modum habitus & qualitatis permanentis: adeoque immerito a Theologis Romanae communionis illis imputari, quod negent dari gratiam aliquam habitualem, & quae sit qualitas in anima inhaerens; cum istud ab Ecclesiae Reformatae Doctoribus vel nullis, vel paucis negetur.
latin.2437: XLVIII. Id vero solum in quaestione est, An in illis scripturae locis ubi dicimur per Dei gratiam servari & justificari, gratia significet externum Dei favorem & benevolentiam: an vero gratiam aliquam quae nobis inhaereat, seu actualis illa sit, sive habitualis. Prius affirmat Schola Reformata, posterius Romana.
latin.2438: XLIX. Ac proinde non quaeritur simpliciter, An Detur aliqua gratia salvifica nobis inhaerens per modum sive actus, sive habitus: sed istud tantum An de ejusmodi gratia intelligenda sint ea scripturae loca ubi salus nostra & justificatio gratiae Dei tribuitur, quod affirmant Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, Reformati vero negant. Quae quaestio quanti sit momenti, alibi fusius a nobis expensum est.

sections.title: Universal and particular grace: Polanus
sections.pass_a: XXVI. Besides many Theologians of the Reformed School are wont to distinguish grace into Universal grace, and particular grace: but not all in the same sense. Polanus in book 2. chapter 21. of his syntagma after at the beginning of the chapter he distinguished grace into that which resides in God, and that which is given by God, toward the end says, Grace given to men by God is either universal, as both natural grace which is given to all and each man, and supernatural grace before the fall: or particular, as supernatural grace after the fall, which is conferred on a part only of the human race.
pass_b: Thesis XXVI. Many theologians of the Reformed school also commonly distinguish grace into universal and particular grace, though not all in the same sense.

In his Syntagma (book 2, chapter 21), Polanus opens the chapter by dividing grace into the grace residing in God and the grace God gives. Near its close he writes that the grace God gives to people is of two sorts. Universal grace includes natural grace, bestowed on everyone without exception, and supernatural grace before the fall. Particular grace is supernatural grace after the fall, granted only to part of humankind.

sections.title: Polanus: natural and supernatural grace, before and after the fall
sections.pass_a: XXVII. For before he distinguished grace into natural, and supernatural. And by natural grace he understands nature itself, and all the gifts both of nature intact, and those which remained in nature corrupted. But by supernatural grace whatever gifts above nature were conferred on men by God. And therefore again he distinguishes supernatural grace into supernatural grace before the fall of man, by which he designates the gifts above nature conferred on man intact: and into supernatural grace after the fall of man, by which name he embraces all the gifts above nature conferred on man a sinner.
pass_b: Thesis XXVII. Earlier he had distinguished grace into natural and supernatural. By natural grace he means nature itself and all the gifts both of unfallen nature and of what remained in corrupted nature. By supernatural grace he means any gifts above nature that God has bestowed on human beings.

So he divides supernatural grace again into supernatural grace before man's fall, meaning the gifts above nature bestowed on man while still whole, and supernatural grace after man's fall, a name that covers all the gifts above nature bestowed on man as a sinner.

sections.title: Polanus: no supernatural grace is universal after the fall
sections.pass_a: XXVIII. Therefore by universal grace he signifies the gifts both natural, and supernatural conferred before sin on the first parents, because namely they pertained to the whole human race, which consisted of them alone, and were to be propagated to all their posterity, if they had persisted in obedience to God. And besides after the corruption of the human race, the benefits and gifts of nature which remained after sin, and are common to all men, he will also have able to be designated by the name of universal grace. But after sin he will have no supernatural gift or benefit to be universal. And therefore after the fall he says all supernatural grace is particular. And accordingly the grace which he calls particular, he distinguishes into that which is common to elect and reprobate, and which is given by God for the salvation of others, such as are the charisms which are called by the Scholastics graces freely given: and into that which is proper to the elect, and is destined for the salvation of those to whom it is given, as are faith, regeneration, repentance, charity, hope of eternal life, the gift of perseverance, which the Scholastics refer to grace making pleasing.
pass_b: Thesis XXVIII. By universal grace, then, he means the gifts, natural as well as supernatural, that were bestowed on our first parents before sin. They belonged to the whole human race, which then consisted of those two alone, and they were to be passed on to all their descendants had they persevered in obedience to God.

He also allows that after the corruption of the human race, the benefits and gifts of nature that remained after sin and are common to all people may be called universal grace. But after sin he admits no supernatural gift or benefit as universal, and so he says that after the fall all supernatural grace is particular.

Accordingly he divides what he calls particular grace into two. One kind is common to elect and reprobate and is given by God for the salvation of others, such as the charisms the scholastics call graces freely given. The other is proper to the elect and meant for the salvation of those who receive it: faith, regeneration, repentance, love, the hope of eternal life and the gift of perseverance, which the scholastics class under grace that makes pleasing.

sections.title: Testard: general grace offers, particular grace applies
sections.pass_a: XXIX. But Paul Testard some years ago Pastor of the Church of Blois in the synopsis of the doctrine on nature and grace, thesis 300. uses the distinction of grace into Particular and Universal in a far different sense. For, he says, grace toward sinners is twofold, General, and Particular. General which is given to the whole world, the Offer and power of salvation. Particular which is of the Elect only, the application of salvation. Of which the nearest foundation is free election: the middle efficacious calling: the crown justification, keeping, glorification. And straightway he says that particular grace is either prevenient, such as is Election and Calling: Or mercifully rewarding, such as is justification, keeping, glorification.
pass_b: Thesis XXIX. Paul Testard, some years ago pastor of the church at Blois, uses the distinction of grace into particular and universal in a very different sense in his synopsis of the doctrine of nature and grace (thesis 300).

Grace toward sinners, he says, is of two kinds, general and particular. General grace is given to the whole world: it is the offer of salvation and the power to be saved. Particular grace belongs to the elect alone: it is the application of salvation. Its nearest foundation is free election, its middle stage effectual calling, and its crown justification, preservation and glorification.
He immediately adds that this particular grace is either prevenient, such as election and calling, or mercifully rewarding, such as justification, preservation and glorification.

sections.title: Testard's universal grace: salvation made possible for all
sections.pass_a: XXX. Therefore from his mind, universal or general grace is that benefit of God by which salvation is offered to all men, and so is rendered possible to all and each of them, that they can be saved, if they will, and it stands only through themselves that they do not obtain salvation. For he thinks God prepared Christ the Redeemer for all, and by his death the sins of all men were so expiated, that on God's part nothing more stands in the way that whoever withdraws from sin, and is converted to God, become partaker of salvation, and be freed from perdition: since to his avenging justice for the sins of all men abundant satisfaction was made by the death of Christ. And not that only, but that God calls all men to participation of salvation in Christ; some indeed by the express word of the Gospel, but others by the voice of creatures, and by various testimonies of divine kindness and patience, which shine in the works of nature and providence, and invite men to repentance, and consequently to salvation.
pass_b: Thesis XXX. In his view, then, universal or general grace is the benefit of God by which salvation is offered to all people and so made possible for each and every one of them: they can be saved if they will, and it is due to themselves alone that they do not obtain salvation.

For he holds that God provided Christ as Redeemer for all, and that by his death the sins of all people were expiated in such a way that, on God's side, nothing further prevents anyone who turns from sin and is converted to God from sharing in salvation and being freed from perdition, since Christ's death made full satisfaction to God's avenging justice for the sins of all.

Nor is that all. He holds that God calls all people to share in salvation in Christ: some by the explicit word of the Gospel, others by the voice of creation and by the many signs of God's kindness and patience that shine out in the works of nature and providence and invite people to repentance, and so to salvation.

sections.title: Testard's particular grace: salvation effectually applied to the elect
sections.pass_a: XXXI. But by particular grace he understands that by which God makes certain of men truly partakers of salvation, not simply offering the benefit of Christ to them, but efficaciously and actually applying it. And he calls that grace particular, because it is not extended to all as the former, but is proper to few, namely the elect, as that which consists in election itself, and the benefits flowing from it: such as are internal and efficacious calling, justification, the gift of perseverance and glorification.
pass_b: Thesis XXXI. By particular grace he means the grace by which God makes certain people actually share in salvation, not merely offering them Christ's benefit but applying it to them effectually and in fact.

He calls this grace particular because, unlike the first, it does not reach everyone but belongs to a few, namely the elect, since it consists in election itself and in the benefits that flow from it: internal and effectual calling, justification, the gift of perseverance and glorification.

sections.title: Amyraut and his followers; the opponents in the Netherlands, France and England
sections.pass_a: XXXII. In the same way that division of grace into particular and universal the most Distinguished man Moses Amyraut uses and explains in those two treatises which he entitled, On universal and particular grace. And with him agree and assent all those in France who follow the Method and doctrine of Cameron, and in Germany and Poland very many, who seek and pursue peace and concord with the Lutherans. But in the Netherlands most of the Reformed, and in France and England not a few disapprove and oppose that distinction, nor do they admit any universal grace of Christ.
pass_b: Thesis XXXII. The very distinguished Moise Amyraut uses and explains this division of grace into particular and universal in the same way in the two treatises he entitled On Universal and Particular Grace.

All those in France who follow Cameron's method and teaching agree with him and support him, as do a great many in Germany and Poland who seek and pursue peace and concord with the Lutherans. But most of the Reformed in the Netherlands, and not a few in France and England, reject and attack this distinction and admit no universal grace of Christ at all.

sections.title: Universal grace is an external benefit; particular grace works within
sections.pass_a: XXXIII. But from what has been said it is plain enough, that those Theologians by the name of universal grace do not understand some grace inhering in men, but only a certain external benefit of God, by which he delivered his son to death, that satisfaction might be made to divine justice for the sins of all men, and by which his justice being thus appeased, he calls men externally to the communion of salvation, which Christ obtained for them by his death. And on the contrary by particular grace they chiefly designate the gifts and helps of God, by which acting inwardly in men he works conversion and faith in them, and at last makes them in fact partakers of eternal salvation.
pass_b: Thesis XXXIII. From what has been said it is clear enough that these theologians do not mean by universal grace any grace inhering in people. They mean only an external benefit of God: he handed his Son over to death so that divine justice might be satisfied for the sins of all, and, his justice being thus appeased, he calls people from outside to share in the salvation that Christ won for them by his death.

By particular grace, on the other hand, they chiefly mean the gifts and helps of God by which he acts within people, works conversion and faith in them, and in the end makes them actually share in eternal salvation.

sections.title: Amyraut: objective and subjective grace
sections.pass_a: XXXIV. Whence arose another distinction of grace, namely into Objective and subjective grace, which that most Distinguished Moses Amyraut hands down, at the beginning of his dissertation on Particular grace. For he teaches there that a twofold grace is necessary for engendering faith in the souls of men. One which holds itself in the manner of an object, of God's mercy offering externally in the satisfaction of Christ: the other which inwardly affects and illuminates the mind, that the object may be admitted. The former he calls objective, because it is external, and of itself posits nothing in man; but is only proposed to him as a certain object, which he ought to embrace by faith. But the latter he calls subjective, because it changes man inwardly, and is received in him as in a subject. And this Objective grace he contends is universal, and pertains to absolutely all men: but subjective grace he teaches is particular, and peculiarly destined for the elect.
pass_b: Thesis XXXIV. This gave rise to another distinction of grace, into objective and subjective grace, which the very distinguished Moise Amyraut sets out at the beginning of his dissertation on particular grace.

There he teaches that two graces are needed to produce faith in human souls. One functions as an object: the mercy of God offering itself from outside in Christ's satisfaction. The other affects and enlightens the mind from within so that the object may be received.

He calls the first objective because it is external and of itself places nothing in a person; it is only set before him as an object that he ought to embrace by faith. He calls the second subjective because it changes a person within and is received in him as in a subject. He holds that objective grace is universal and belongs to absolutely everyone, while subjective grace is particular and meant specially for the elect.

lemmas.gloss: a twofold grace is necessary for faith

sections.title: The Remonstrants philosophize about grace like the Molinists
sections.pass_a: XXXV. Further those who in the Netherlands are called Remonstrants or Arminians, philosophize about grace in almost the same way, as those of the Doctors of the Roman School who today are called Molinists. For they use distinctions of grace into exciting and helping, preventing and subsequent, operating and cooperating with the same sense with which those [use them], as it is permitted to see in the declaration of the sentence of the Remonstrants about the article third and fourth, which is had in their Synod.
pass_b: Thesis XXXV. Those in the Netherlands called Remonstrants or Arminians reason about grace in much the same way as the doctors of the Roman school now called Molinists.

For they use the distinctions of grace into rousing and assisting, prevenient and subsequent, and operating and cooperating grace, and in the same sense as those doctors. This can be seen in the Remonstrants' declaration of their opinion on the third and fourth articles, which is contained in their synod.

sections.title: Remonstrant rousing grace: illumination of the mind acting on the will
sections.pass_a: XXXVI. For there they say they understand by rousing grace the gracious and unmerited operation of God and the Holy Spirit, which first imbues the intellect with the knowledge of saving things, and illumines it, and so makes it assent to divine truth, and secondly acts on the will itself through the same illumination and the senses comprised in the word.
pass_b: Thesis XXXVI. There they say that by rousing grace they mean the gracious and unmerited working of God and the Holy Spirit.

First it fills the intellect with knowledge of the things of salvation and enlightens it, and so brings it to assent to divine truth. Second, it acts on the will itself through that same enlightenment and through the meanings contained in the word.

sections.title: Remonstrants: the Spirit acts on the will, but not irresistibly
sections.pass_a: XXXVII. They add however that they by no means deny that the Holy Spirit acts immediately on the will, by infusing into it strength and supernatural power to believe, by which power however the will is not necessitated, and irresistibly determined. And they note that this grace is called rousing, because it draws, allures, invites, and incites the will to free assent, and, man not placing an obstacle, makes it will in act. And that the same grace is also called prevenient, because it goes before our will: and finally Operating, because it is also the cause of volition.
pass_b: Thesis XXXVII. Still, they add, they do not in the least deny a direct working of the Holy Spirit on the will, in which he pours into it the strength and supernatural ability to believe. That ability, though, neither forces the will nor settles its choice irresistibly.

They note that this grace is called rousing because it draws, attracts, invites and urges the will toward free assent and, provided the person puts no obstacle in the way, makes it actually will. The same grace is also called prevenient, because it goes before our will, and finally operating, because it is also the cause of the act of willing.

sections.title: Why rousing grace is needed: supernatural acts exceed the will's native power
sections.pass_a: XXXVIII. And they warn that the necessity of this grace arises from this, that supernatural acts, such as are those in which the conversion of man consists, far exceed the inborn and innate power of the will, and therefore supernatural strength, and special grace, going before the very act of the will, is needed to elicit it; which is not needed for other natural acts of the will proportioned to its power.
pass_b: Thesis XXXVIII. They point out that the need for this grace arises because supernatural acts, such as those that make up a person's conversion, far exceed the will's inborn and native power.

So supernatural strength and a special grace that goes before the act of the will itself are needed to produce such an act, which is not the case for the will's other, natural acts that are proportioned to its power.

sections.title: Remonstrant assisting grace: concurrence 'more than moral'
sections.pass_a: XXXIX. But assisting grace to them is that which helps the will, and effectively concurs with it to produce the act; and that not morally only, but also Physically, or rather more than morally: because namely the word Physically seems to them very inconvenient in this business, on account of the supernaturality of the acts which are in question: nor yet does another proper word occur by which they may express this positively. And they observe that this grace is also called cooperating, because it works with the will; and subsequent in respect of prevenient and rousing grace.
pass_b: Thesis XXXIX. Assisting grace, for them, is the grace that helps the will and concurs with it effectively in producing the act, and does so not only morally but also physically, or rather more than morally.

For the word 'physically' seems to them most unsuitable in this matter, because the acts in question are supernatural; yet no other proper word occurs by which they could state the point positively. They observe that this grace is also called cooperating, because it works together with the will, and subsequent in relation to prevenient and rousing grace.

sections.title: Remonstrants reject habitual grace infused without our acts
sections.pass_a: XL. As regards the distinction of grace into actual and habitual, it is rejected by them, as a figment of the Scholastics, which has no foundation in scripture. Provided however there be understood by habitual grace such an infusion of faith, hope and charity into the will, that without any intervening operation of the will man be said to obtain those habits. For they think that through frequent acts of faith, hope and charity proceeding from the special grace of God, at length habitual faith, charity and hope are produced in us: as through repeated acts of justice and liberality the habits of liberality and justice are produced in us. But to think that the habits of the Theological virtues are produced immediately by God without man's own operation, belongs to those who wish all those habits to be infused all at once, which they judge too laborious to acquire by frequent acts.
pass_b: Thesis XL. The distinction of grace into actual and habitual they reject as a scholastic invention with no basis in scripture, provided that habitual grace is taken to mean an infusion of faith, hope and love into the will such that a person is said to acquire those habits without any intervening act of the will.

For they hold that habitual faith, love and hope are finally produced in us through frequent acts of faith, hope and love that come from God's special grace, just as habits of liberality and justice are produced in us through repeated acts of justice and liberality.

To think that the habits of the theological virtues are produced directly by God without any act of the person's own is, they say, the view of people who want all those habits poured into them at one stroke, because they find it too much labour to acquire them by frequent acts.

sections.title: Yet they admit an infused permanent supernatural power
sections.pass_a: XLI. But if one please to understand by habitual grace a certain supernatural power granted to the will to this end that it can believe and act well, they profess that they willingly admit it. Whence it is plain that they, although they deny habitual grace, yet acknowledge a certain permanent quality, and supernatural power which is infused through grace. Which falls back almost to the same thing, and differs little or nothing from the opinion of those who speak otherwise.
pass_b: Thesis XLI. But if habitual grace is taken to mean a supernatural power given to the will so that it can believe and act well, they declare that they gladly accept it.

So it is clear that, although they deny habitual grace, they still acknowledge a permanent quality and supernatural power infused by grace. That comes to almost the same thing and differs little or not at all from the view of those who speak differently.

sections.title: Both sides grant both senses of grace; mutual accusations are groundless
sections.pass_a: XLII. However from those things which have been set out by us hitherto about the various divisions and senses of grace, both in the Roman School, and in the Reformed School, it is manifest that the Theologians of the Rom. Church of their own accord teach and grant that grace in sacred scripture is not always taken for certain gifts and helps of God inhering in us, but that by grace is sometimes understood the very favour of God, whence those gifts and helps proceed. And in turn that the Reformed Doctors do not deny that in scripture the name of grace is often attributed to the gifts and effects of divine favour. And therefore in vain some Reformed accuse the Doctors of the Roman School, as though they would have nothing else ever understood by grace than some supernatural gift infused into us. And on the contrary without reason the Doctors of the Roman School harass the Reformed, and complain of them, as though they acknowledged no grace inhering in us.
pass_b: Thesis XLII. From what we have set out so far about the various divisions and senses of grace in both the Roman and the Reformed school, it is plain that the theologians of the Roman Church freely teach and grant that in holy scripture grace is not always taken for gifts and helps of God that inhere in us, and that grace sometimes means God's favour itself, from which those gifts and helps come.
In turn, the Reformed doctors do not deny that scripture often gives the name of grace to the gifts and effects of God's favour.

So some of the Reformed are wrong to accuse the doctors of the Roman school of meaning nothing by grace but some supernatural gift infused into us. And the doctors of the Roman school have no reason to attack the Reformed and complain of them as if they acknowledged no grace inhering in us.

sections.title: Grace freely given: only a dispute about words
sections.pass_a: XLIII. Moreover it is plain from what was said about the distinction of grace into freely given and making pleasing, that it is nothing but a contest about words. For what the Reformed contend, that there is no grace which is not freely given, and that all grace is therefore called grace because it is gratuitously given, is admitted by the Doctors of the Roman School, who warn that a certain species of grace is singularly called by them grace freely given: not because the other species of grace is not also freely given; but because it seemed convenient to the School to call that species by the name of the genus, because it lacks a proper name.
pass_b: Thesis XLIII. It is also clear from what was said about the distinction of grace into grace freely given and grace that makes pleasing that this is nothing but a dispute about words.

The Reformed contend that no grace is given otherwise than freely, and that every grace is called grace precisely because it is given gratuitously. The doctors of the Roman school accept this. They explain that they call one species of grace grace freely given in a special sense, not because the other species is not freely given too, but because the school found it convenient to call that species by the name of the genus, since it has no name of its own.

sections.title: Grace that makes pleasing does not precede God's love
sections.pass_a: XLIV. But the other species of grace the same Doctors do not therefore name grace making pleasing, because it should precede every act of divine love toward us, and be the cause by which God first is moved that he may will well to us; which the Reformed rightly judge false and absurd: since God loves us before we love him.
pass_b: Thesis XLIV. When these doctors name the other species grace that makes pleasing, their reason is not that it precedes every act of divine love toward us, or that it is the cause by which God is first moved to wish us well.
The Reformed rightly judge that to be false and absurd, since God loves us before we love him.

sections.title: The Reformed grant that faith makes one pleasing to God
sections.pass_a: XLV. Nor yet on that account does the Reformed School deny that what the Roman understands by the name of grace making pleasing, namely faith, hope and charity, is something by reason of which man is pleasing and acceptable to God in a certain singular way, looking to which Paul to the Hebrews says, It is impossible without faith to please God. To which the Theologians of the Roman Church look, when they call that grace making pleasing.
pass_b: Thesis XLV. Yet the Reformed school does not therefore deny that what the Roman school means by grace that makes pleasing, namely faith, hope and love, is something on account of which a person is pleasing and acceptable to God in a special way.

Paul has this in view when he says to the Hebrews that without faith it is impossible to please God, and the theologians of the Roman Church have the same in view when they call that grace the grace that makes pleasing.

sections.title: God's love both precedes the gifts and follows them
sections.pass_a: XLVI. And so both will easily grant that there is some act of divine love which precedes those gifts and virtues, which the Scholastics designate by the name of grace making pleasing: because namely, God wills us well before we have them: and at the same time that there is a certain act of the same love which such gifts precede, namely because without them we cannot please God and be approved by him. But such gifts and virtues formally constitute the man who is adorned with them pleasing and acceptable to God. According to that of Peter Acts tenth, In truth I have found that God is not a respecter of persons: but in every nation he who fears him, and works righteousness, is accepted by him.
pass_b: Thesis XLVI. So both sides will readily grant that there is an act of God's love that comes before the gifts and virtues the scholastics call grace that makes pleasing, since God wishes us well before we have them. They will also grant that there is an act of the same love that those gifts come before, since without them we cannot please God or win his approval.

Such gifts and virtues formally make the person adorned with them pleasing and acceptable to God. As Peter says in Acts 10: Truly I have found that God shows no partiality, but in every nation whoever fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.

sections.title: The Reformed admit infused habits; the charge against them is unjust
sections.pass_a: XLVII. Next it is plain from those things which were set out before, that the Doctors of the Reformed School admit certain virtues divinely infused, and certain gifts of saving grace, which are in the soul by way of habit and permanent quality: and so it is undeservedly imputed to them by the Theologians of the Roman communion, that they deny that there is given some habitual grace, and which is a quality inhering in the soul; since that is denied by either none, or few of the Doctors of the Reformed Church.
pass_b: Thesis XLVII. Next, it is clear from what was set out earlier that the doctors of the Reformed school admit certain divinely infused virtues and certain gifts of saving grace that exist in the soul as a habit and permanent quality.

So the theologians of the Roman communion unjustly charge them with denying that there is any habitual grace that is a quality inhering in the soul, since few or none of the doctors of the Reformed Church deny it.

sections.title: The real question: what 'grace' means in the texts on salvation
sections.pass_a: XLVIII. But this only is in question, Whether in those places of scripture where we are said to be saved and justified by the grace of God, grace signifies the external favour and benevolence of God: or some grace which inheres in us, whether that be actual, or habitual. The former the Reformed School affirms, the latter the Roman.
pass_b: Thesis XLVIII. The only point in question is this. In the passages of scripture that say we are saved and justified by God's grace, does grace mean God's external favour and goodwill, or some grace that inheres in us, whether actual or habitual?
The Reformed school affirms the first, the Roman school the second.

sections.title: Not whether inherent grace exists, but how to read those texts; locus closed
sections.pass_a: XLIX. And accordingly it is not asked simply, Whether there is given some saving grace inhering in us by way either of act, or of habit: but this only Whether of grace of this kind are to be understood those places of scripture where our salvation and justification is attributed to the grace of God, which the Doctors of the Roman Church affirm, but the Reformed deny. Of how great moment this question is, has been weighed more fully by us elsewhere.
pass_b: Thesis XLIX. So the question is not simply whether there is a saving grace that inheres in us, either as an act or as a habit. It is only whether the passages of scripture that ascribe our salvation and justification to God's grace are to be understood of such grace.
The doctors of the Roman Church say yes and the Reformed say no. How much this question matters we have considered more fully elsewhere.
